evidence: Confirmed the exact mechanism before fixing it: backend_app/main.py's health() handler always returns HTTP 200 from /health -- it computes 'status': 'ok'/'degraded' from Redis/Supabase/QuestDB probes, but that result lives only in the JSON body. terraform/alb.tf's aws_lb_target_group.api health_check is a bare status-code matcher (matcher = "200"), which never reads the body, so a target with no reachable database or Redis still passed every ALB health check and kept receiving production traffic. backend_app/core/readiness.py's evaluate_readiness (added under OBS-01, confirmed by reading its module docstring and the /health/ready route) actually measures the database (every authenticated request resolves identity and RLS through it) and Redis (backs the rate limiter and the distributed execution locks outside a declared local environment) and returns a real 503 when either is down -- QuestDB/telemetry deliberately excluded, since it degrades to a mock by design and must not turn a metrics outage into a total one. Changed aws_lb_target_group.api's health_check.path from /health to /health/ready; left timeout at 5s (readiness.py's own PROBE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is 3.0s per dependency, comfortably inside it) and matcher at "200" unchanged (503 correctly fails it). Left the websocket target group's /health/live (a different service, ws_server.py, already covered by WS-01) and the frontend target group's "/" untouched -- only the API target group's path was wrong. New tests/test_inf01_alb_health_check_targets_readiness.py (2 tests, direct text parsing of terraform/alb.tf since no terraform binary is available in this sandbox): the API target group's health_check.path is exactly /health/ready (not a substring check -- /health is itself a substring of /health/ready, so a naive check would be satisfied by the very regression this guards against) and matcher stays "200"; a second test pins the timeout staying >= 5s against readiness.py's own probe budget. Verified as a real regression test: git-stashed just the terraform/alb.tf change and reran, got the exact expected failure ('expected ... /health/ready, got /health instead'); restored and reran, green. Full regression: tests/test_inf01_alb_health_check_targets_readiness.py (2 passed) + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped). terraform/alb.tf parses as valid HCL (python-hcl2; no terraform binary available in this sandbox for a real plan/validate). evidence: This finding's remaining_action has two halves; investigated both. (1) 'Remove dead files': grepped every .tf file for `file(`/`templatefile(` and literal filenames; found terraform/route53-policy.json (a bare IAM policy JSON, no project-specific resource IDs) referenced nowhere -- not by terraform, not by any script/workflow/doc except a historical git-ls-tree-style inventory snapshot in staging/p11b22_entry_staged.txt that is itself just a listing. Removed in commit bfec458 as unambiguous dead weight. Also checked terraform/redis-only/main.tf, which LOOKS like a second dead-file candidate (a whole directory alongside the root module's own redis.tf) but is almost certainly the OPPOSITE: it is a SEPARATE, standalone root module (its own terraform{}/provider{} blocks) with hardcoded real resource identifiers (vpc-0f3e7b3f243fbc133, a real security group ID sg-0262aed02d8df0356, real subnet CIDRs) and an explicit `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true; ignore_changes = all }` guard on a replication group it calls 'deprecated' -- exactly the kind of guard someone writes around a REAL, already-existing production resource, not a throwaway file. It most likely IS the one accurate terraform description of how production Redis was actually provisioned (hardcoded against the real existing VPC/SG, applied as its own standalone `terraform apply` from a different working directory/state), predating and never consolidated into the root module's own generic, environment-parameterized redis.tf -- itself likely never actually applied to real production. This is a direct, concrete illustration of the finding's own title ('terraform does not describe the production deployment' -- there are TWO different terraform descriptions of Redis in this repository, and nothing says which one, if either, matches what AWS actually runs). Did NOT delete it -- confirming which file (if either) is accurate needs real AWS access this sandbox does not have, and deleting on a wrong guess would destroy the only record this repo has of real infrastructure. (2) 'Import live resources into Terraform state': needs real AWS credentials to run `terraform import` against the actual account -- genuinely unreachable from this sandbox.

title: Background schedulers run in every web worker
evidence: Confirmed in main.py: start_reconciliation_scheduler() is called from the FastAPI lifespan startup hook, which every uvicorn/gunicorn web worker process runs independently -- so every worker built its own ReconciliationScheduler (core/reconciliation_scheduler.py) and polled the shared reconciliation_mismatches table every POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS (30s) from N processes at once, each attempting to escalate the same mismatches and trigger the same kill switch redundantly. Checked RECON-01 first to confirm this is a DIFFERENT, already-running scheduler from ExchangeReconciliationService (RECON-01's subject, never started anywhere) -- did not touch RECON-01's deliberately-deferred leader-election/tenant-enumeration work, only this already-running one. Neither duplicated action was itself corrupted (the kill switch and the 'already-escalated' DB check are each idempotent on their own), so the real cost was DB/alerting load multiplied by N for no benefit. Fixed by adding _try_become_leader: a renewable Redis lease using the exact same primitive master_executor's execution lock and IdempotentExchangeSubmission.claim_submission already use (SET key value NX EX to win an unheld lease; a plain SET to renew one still held by the SAME instance id, checked via GET first, since a one-shot NX-only lock would make even the current leader lose and re-win the role every cycle). Fails CLOSED the same way those two already do -- redis_manager.get_client() returning None or raising answers 'not leader' rather than letting a per-process mock stand in for Redis outside development and silently reintroduce the N-way fan-out, exactly the failure mode tests/test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py already guards the other two locks against. _loop now calls _poll_and_escalate only when leader. New tests/test_inf04_reconciliation_scheduler_leader_election.py (8 tests) against a fake Redis client backed by a store SHARED across instances (unlike MockRedisClient's per-process dict): exactly one of two schedulers wins leadership in the same cycle; the same leader renews rather than losing the role every cycle; a different instance cannot steal an active lease; a crashed leader's expired lease is picked up by another instance; Redis unreachable/erroring both fail closed; a non-leader cycle skips _poll_and_escalate entirely while a leader cycle runs it. Full regression: 6 existing reconciliation/health test files + test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py (75 passed); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).

Each category reports its own ok/error so one failing table does not abort the export. delete_account(supabase, user_id, user) is deliberately NOT a physical cascade-delete across this repository's ~58 tables -- auditing which may legally and safely be hard-deleted without a real Postgres instance to verify against is exactly the kind of repo-wide change this session has consistently declined to improvise (the same reasoning TENANT-01's FORCE RLS wiring and RECON-01's leader election were left to a dedicated session over, cross-referenced directly in the module's own docstring). Instead it composes existing, already-tested primitives: stops every live deployment (strategy_lifecycle.stop_deployments_for_reason, the same Requirement 20.9 path the kill switch already uses), stops every RUNNING/PAUSED paper session (paper_session_service.stop_session, called the way it is already designed to be called without a live feed/task handle), revokes every connected exchange's API keys (APIKeyVault.delete_exchange_keys), and anonymises the profile's PII fields while setting is_frozen=True -- the same flag core.dependencies.get_current_user already enforces as a 403 everywhere, achieving the functional equivalent of account deletion with no new column and no migration. The profile anonymisation step is the one allowed to raise (a row that cannot be updated means the account is not deleted); the other three steps are best-effort and individually reported. Two new routes: GET /api/user/account/export and DELETE /api/user/account, the latter requiring an exact confirmation phrase in the body (422 otherwise) since there is no undo for the PII anonymisation. New tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py (9 tests): export reads every direct table scoped to the user and never includes decrypted credentials; a failing category does not abort the export; deletion stops deployments, stops only RUNNING/PAUSED sessions (not CREATED/STOPPED), revokes every connected exchange's keys, anonymises the profile; deletion raises when the profile update matches no row; one exchange failing to revoke does not stop profile anonymisation; the export route requires auth; the delete route rejects a wrong confirmation phrase and succeeds with the exact one. Registered the new DELETE route in test_validation_sweep.py's exhaustive MUTATING_ROUTES list (its own self-enforcing coverage check caught the omission on first run). Full regression: test_user_router.py + test_validation_sweep.py (387 passed, 2 skipped). ADDITIONALLY this session: used this session's own newly-provisioned real Postgres replica (see TENANT-01's entry) to audit, for the first time with an actual schema rather than source inspection alone, exactly what a literal `DELETE FROM profiles WHERE id = ...` would do. Querying information_schema for every foreign key referencing profiles(id) found 27 referencing columns across 26 tables: 20 CASCADE (dag_tasks, exchange_connections, exchange_keys, execution_records, fills, notification_settings, orders, positions, referral_codes/_commissions/_payouts/_profiles/_relationships/_wallets, referrals, risk_settings, strategy_limits), 1 SET NULL (profiles.referred_by_user_id, a self-reference), and -- the finding that matters here -- 6 RESTRICT: billing_invoices, invoices, payment_methods, risk_settings_audit, security_logs, subscriptions. A real physical delete of the profiles row would FAIL OUTRIGHT on any of those 6 while a single row remains, by the database's own constraint, not silently leave orphans. This confirms the current anonymise-and-revoke implementation's reasoning is not merely 'safe because this sandbox lacked Postgres to verify against' -- it is the ARCHITECTURALLY CORRECT choice independent of that: making a real hard-delete work would mean either resolving those 6 tables' own rows first (destroying exactly the audit/financial history BILL-01, AUD-01 and SEC-xx's own findings in this same ledger depend on existing durably -- security_logs and risk_settings_audit by name) or relaxing their RESTRICT constraints (which would re-open exactly the kind of accidental data loss those constraints exist to prevent). If the product's actual legal/compliance requirement is physical erasure rather than anonymisation + access revocation, the real design question a future session should resolve is narrower than before: not 'can we cascade-delete 58 tables' but specifically 'what should happen to these 6 financial/audit tables' historical rows under an erasure request' -- a business/legal policy question (does erasure override retention?), not a technical blocker, and one this sandbox does not have the authority to answer on its own. RESOLVED this session: asked the product owner directly whether the real legal/compliance obligation requires physical erasure of historical data on account deletion, or whether anonymising PII + revoking access while retaining financial/audit history (this entry's existing implementation) is sufficient. Answer: anonymisation + access revocation IS sufficient. This was the one open question this entry's own remaining_action named as blocking closure -- with it answered, the existing implementation (export_account_data / delete_account in backend/account_lifecycle.py, 9 tests in tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py, both already built and tested in an earlier pass this remediation effort) meets the real requirement as designed. The FK-constraint audit against this session's own real Postgres replica (see above) independently confirmed the same conclusion from the schema side: 6 tables RESTRICT a physical delete outright while they hold financial/audit history for that user, so a hard-delete implementation would have had to either destroy that history or fight those constraints -- neither necessary now that anonymisation is confirmed sufficient.
remaining_action: None. The one open question (does the real legal/compliance requirement exceed anonymisation + access revocation) has been answered by the product owner: no, the current implementation already meets the real requirement. No further action needed.

title: Privilege-hardening backstop does not detect RLS-disabled customer tables
evidence: Confirmed the defect by reading scripts/post_migration_validation.py section 3 ("VALIDATING RLS STATUS"): it checked rowsecurity only for tables already named in the required_tables list defined at the top of the same function -- the same list section 1 checks for existence. A table a later migration grants anon or authenticated a privilege on (Supabase grants most new tables a default privilege shape automatically) but never gets ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY would not be examined at all unless someone also remembered to add its name to this list -- the exact gap the title names. Separately, the script never called sys.exit(1) despite importing sys, so even a FAILED line printed to stdout left the process exiting 0. Fixed both: fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls(cur) now asks the catalog directly (pg_tables joined against information_schema.table_privileges for grantee IN ('anon','authenticated')) for every table either role can touch, with no table name hardcoded anywhere; evaluate_privilege_hardening(rows) is the pure decision half (same fetch/evaluate split already used in scripts/verify_rls.py), and validate_production_db() now returns that result, with __main__ calling sys.exit(1) when it fails. VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRESQL 16 SERVER (this session's own local instance): created a table named db03_brand_new_customer_table_not_on_any_list -- confirmed absent from required_tables by inspecting validate_production_db's own source -- granted authenticated SELECT on it with RLS left disabled, and proved the new check finds it anyway (fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls returns it; evaluate_privilege_hardening fails). Negative controls: enabling RLS on that same table makes the check pass; a table with no anon/authenticated grant at all is never flagged even with RLS disabled (service-only tables are a normal, intentional configuration). New tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_detects_untracked_tables_postgres.py (4 tests, real Postgres) and tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_pure_logic.py (5 tests, no database) all passed. tests/test_migration_tooling.py (36 tests, pre-existing, covers this same file's import-of-os regression) still passes.
remaining_action: Not wired into any CI workflow (grepped .github/ -- no match), and was not before this fix either; it remains a manually-run script. A dedicated session should add it as a CI gate run against a disposable Postgres instance, or against staging before a production migration is promoted. Sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 of the same script (table existence, column existence, RPC existence, security-definer check, metadata export) were not touched -- this finding names only the RLS/privilege check's detection gap, not those checks' own exit-code behavior.

title: A paper fill is seven separate PostgREST writes with no transaction and no repair
evidence: Read paper_simulator.apply_fill's own extensive docstring ('THE WRITES, AND THE ORDERING THE MISSING TRANSACTION FORCES') before changing anything: the 7-write sequence is already a deliberate, carefully-reasoned design -- the fill row is written first as the idempotency anchor so a crash before the account UPDATE can be RESUMED rather than lost or double-applied, and a crash past that point is reported as PaperConcurrencyExhausted(partial_write=True) and never retried, because a retry would double-apply money. The docstring states plainly that 'Requirement 24.6's single transaction is not achievable over this transport'. This is a considered tradeoff, not an oversight, and this fix does not revisit it -- doing so would mean second-guessing a documented architectural decision without understanding the full 'not achievable over this transport' constraint, which is exactly the kind of risky, superficial-looking-but-actually-regressive change this session's mandate is to avoid. The real, fixable gap was the 'no repair' half: a partial-write failure's detail reaches only the one HTTP caller of the one request that hit it, with nothing durable recorded, so a dropped connection or an inattentive caller left the affected session undiscoverable afterward. paper_replay.replay already exists (built for Requirement 15.4's audit trail) and independently rebuilds a session's final state from its append-only event/order log, but was unused outside its own module and tests -- there was no counterpart projecting the LIVE rows in a comparable shape, which Reconstruction.as_dict's own docstring anticipates ('a reconstruction and a projection of the stored rows... compare with a bare =='). title: Any access_token in the URL hash becomes the session (login CSRF)
evidence: Confirmed the defect directly in algo22-terminal/src/App.jsx: getEffectiveToken() (read by both AuthGuard and GuestGuard, so on every protected and every guest-only route) checked window.location.hash for access_token= on ANY path and, if not demonstrably expired, silently adopted it into sessionStorage -- a non-expired token proves only that Supabase signed it for SOMEONE, not that it was issued to this browser or that this page load is a legitimate redirect. PasswordRecoveryHandler's own non-recovery access_token= branch had the identical defect, unconditionally (storing the token before even checking the path, let alone expiry). Confirmed Google OAuth (signInWithOAuth) and magic-link OTP (signInWithOtp) are both real, offered sign-in methods (AuthPage.jsx), so this hash-handling could not simply be deleted. Confirmed config.js::getAuthRedirectUrl is the SINGLE redirect target Supabase is ever told to use for every OTP/sign-up/resend/OAuth call site (AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH = '/app/dashboard'), and that no resetPasswordForEmail call with an explicit redirectTo exists anywhere in src/ (so the recovery email's landing path is NOT controlled by this frontend and cannot be safely allowlisted). Fixed by requiring window.location.pathname to be one of the paths Supabase is actually ever told to redirect to (AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH/signin/signup/root) before either call site honours a hash access_token; also added the missing expiry check to PasswordRecoveryHandler's two branches. New tests/unit/authHashLandingPath.test.jsx (4 tests, vitest): the allowlist accepts exactly the four legitimate paths and rejects an arbitrary in-app page; a direct exercise of getEffectiveToken() proves a hash token on a disallowed path is never stored or returned, and the identical token on the real redirect path IS adopted (proving this narrows, not removes, the feature). Pre-existing auth suites (auth_otp/auth_oauth/authRedirectOrigin, 52 tests) still pass unchanged.
remaining_action: This narrows the attack from 'any page in the app' to 'the one path Supabase is told to redirect to', but does NOT make the underlying implicit OAuth/magic-link flow itself CSRF-proof: an attacker can still craft a link landing on AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH itself (https://<app>/app/dashboard#access_token=<attacker's own valid token>) and a victim clicking it still adopts the attacker's session. The complete fix is PKCE (flowType: 'pkce' on the Supabase client), which binds the callback to a locally-held code_verifier an attacker cannot forge -- but switching flowType changes the redirect format for every auth path (OAuth, magic link, sign-up, AND the password-recovery email this frontend does not even control the redirect for) and is a live-Supabase-project-config change this sandboxed session has no live project or OAuth provider credentials to test end-to-end. Explicitly not attempted, to avoid shipping an untested change to the only path into the product. The type=recovery branch's landing path is not allowlisted at all, for the stated reason (this frontend never sets its redirectTo), and remains exposed to the same class of attack without narrowing.

title: The web app is served without a Content-Security-Policy
evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/index.html and .github/workflows/06-frontend-deploy.yml: this SPA is built by Vite and synced straight to an S3 bucket behind CloudFront (no origin server at request time, unlike the API's own SecurityHeadersMiddleware in backend_app/main.py, which already sends a tightened nonce+hash CSP but only on backend-served responses) -- index.html carried no CSP at all, meta or header, and could not easily be given one without weakening it: three inline <script> blocks (local-dev detection, a Sentry loader, a GA/Clarity loader) would have forced 'unsafe-inline' into script-src the moment a CSP was added, which defeats most of what a CSP is for. Fixed both problems together. (1) The three inline scripts moved verbatim (same isDummy/local-detection/loader logic, now reading import.meta.env.VITE_* instead of index.html's %VITE_X% token substitution -- equivalent at build time, Vite's native mechanism either way) into algo22-terminal/src/bootstrap.js, a same-origin ES module loaded via <script type="module" src="/src/bootstrap.js"> ahead of main.jsx -- already covered by script-src 'self' with no extra grant needed. (2) index.html now carries <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> with script-src 'self' plus only the origins this build actually loads scripts from (confirmed by grep of src/: js.sentry-cdn.com, www.googletagmanager.com, www.clarity.ms, checkout.razorpay.com for the one real payment path this platform has -- Stripe origins deliberately excluded, since src/pages/Billing.jsx documents this deployment has no live Stripe secret and every Stripe-only endpoint 500s by design) -- no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval anywhere in the policy. connect-src covers every API-hostname topology the deploy workflow's own allow-list names (same-origin CloudFront proxy, api.vyomquant.in, or the raw CloudFront domain) plus the wildcarded Supabase, Sentry, Clarity and GA hosts the app actually calls. A meta-tag CSP cannot carry frame-ancestors/sandbox/report-uri (browsers ignore those three outside an HTTP header per the HTML spec) -- documented in index.html's own comment and left to INF-02 (terraform does not describe the production deployment; a CloudFront response-headers policy is the real fix for that gap, and this session has no AWS credentials to apply one even if terraform described the live distribution). New tests/unit/csp_fe02.test.js (11 tests): the CSP meta tag exists; script-src is 'self' plus https-only named origins with no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval and no directive left empty; every remaining <script> tag in index.html either names a same-origin src or is the non-executable application/ld+json block (browsers do not run it as script and CSP's script-src does not gate it); bootstrap.js loads before main.jsx in document order; bootstrap.js's isDummyValue/detectLocal/runBootstrap reproduce the exact old inline-script behaviour (dummy/placeholder/test/unset id -> harmless local-only stub and no third-party script injected; a real-looking id -> the real Sentry/GA/Clarity loader script injected with that id). `npm run build` with the real Vite config still produces a working dist/index.html carrying the CSP meta tag and zero occurrences of VITE_SENTRY_DSN/VITE_GA_TRACKING_ID/VITE_CLARITY_PROJECT_ID (confirming the token substitution moved to bootstrap.js's bundled output correctly, verified by grepping the emitted entry chunk for __VQ_LOCAL__/clarity.ms/sentry-cdn, all present).
remaining_action: This closes the "served without a CSP" gap in the one place this session can reach (the committed index.html). NOT done: a CloudFront response-headers policy or ALB header (the HTTP-header form of CSP, which alone can add frame-ancestors for real clickjacking protection and survives even if a future edit strips the meta tag) -- that is infrastructure this session has no AWS credentials to touch and that INF-02 already records as undescribed by the repo's own terraform. The remediation note's 'attach WAF, enable logging' half is unchanged for the same reason.

title: A settlement retried after a partial failure can leave money recorded as settled while the buyer's subscription stays unpaid
evidence: Confirmed the real bug first by reading settle()/_settle_once()'s own exhaustive docstrings: a transient failure WITHIN one settle() call's retry loop already resumes correctly via the in-memory _Attempt state (proven by the existing test_a_transient_failure_is_resumed_rather_than_restarted). The gap is cross-call: when an entire settle() invocation exhausts its own retry budget (or the process dies) after the ledger row (step 2) was written but before the transition (step 3) / entitlement (step 4) completed, a later, independent call for the same provider_reference -- a genuine webhook redelivery, with no memory of the first attempt -- found the row via uq_settlement_reference_reversal, read that alone as 'already settled', and returned DUPLICATE_IGNORED without ever checking whether the Subscription had actually been activated. Also established, by reading routers/library.py::check_deployment_permission's own docstring, that deployment_permissions (what grant_deployment_permission/step 4 writes) is advisory-only -- the real gate POST /{library_id}/deploy actually admits on is entitlement_resolver.resolve, which reads library_subscriptions.status/period_expiry directly -- so the step that actually matters for 'is the buyer unlocked' is the transition (step 3), narrowing and de-risking the fix considerably. Fixed in _settle_once's duplicate-at-the-ledger branch (reached only when state.insert_issued is false -- insert_issued being true is the existing, already-correct within-call case): re-read the Subscription fresh and compute whether the transition is still pending the same way _apply_transition decides its own `permitted`, deliberately WITHOUT its renewal_in_place addition for a payment -- an already-active row is indistinguishable there between 'this exact settlement already activated it' and 'a separate, later renewal already extended it', and resuming would risk extending one payment's period a second time, so that case is left untouched by construction rather than guessed at. Every other case (not yet active, already refunded, a reversal re-delivered after its own refund landed) is resolved by _apply_transition's own existing `permitted` check with no such ambiguity. When resumable, falls through to steps 3/4 instead of returning, backfilling settlement_id from the pre-existing row (new _read_settlement_id helper). New StrategyAuditAction.MARKETPLACE_SETTLEMENT_DUPLICATE_RESUMED and _audit_duplicate_resumed, fired instead of DUPLICATE_IGNORED so an operator can see a stuck settlement was completed rather than reading a silent, misleading no-op. New tests/test_mkt03_settlement_resumes_across_redeliveries.py (5 tests, against the real FakeSupabase double this module's own suite uses): the core case (ledger row written, transition exhausted its retry budget, a fresh redelivery completes it, exactly one ledger row/transition row/entitlement grant, the DUPLICATE_RESUMED audit fires -- this test fails before the fix); the counter-test that a redelivery of an already-fully-applied settlement still reports DUPLICATE_IGNORED and touches nothing; the deliberately-excluded already-active case stays unresumed and the period is not re-extended; both mirrored for a reversal. title: A unique index keyed on strategy_id blocks every subscriber after the first from ever deploying a marketplace listing
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/migrations/021_strategy_deployment_live_uniqueness.sql and backend_app/routers/library.py::deploy_marketplace_strategy together. 021 built uq_strategy_deployments_one_live, a partial UNIQUE INDEX ON strategy_deployments (strategy_id) WHERE status IN (<nine live spellings>), to stop an OWNER's own deploy call racing itself into two live rows for one strategy -- correct for a first-party deployment, where strategy_id already uniquely names the owner. deploy_marketplace_strategy writes every SUBSCRIBER's deployment row with strategy_id = owner_strategy_id (the Listing's owner strategy, shared across every subscriber, by design -- so a subscriber executes the owner's immutable version server-side rather than holding a copy of it) and user_id = the subscriber. So the first subscriber's live deployment occupied the only unique slot that strategy_id could ever grant, and every OTHER subscriber's deploy INSERT failed with 23505 unique_violation for as long as that first row stayed live -- a Listing with more than one concurrent subscriber was unusable by all but the first. Fixed exactly per this finding's first suggested remediation: new migration backend_app/migrations/044_mkt04_rekey_live_deployment_uniqueness.sql drops 021's index and recreates it as uq_strategy_deployments_one_live_per_user ON strategy_deployments (user_id, strategy_id), same nine-spelling predicate. This is a WIDER key under the identical predicate, not a different invariant: two rows that already satisfied uniqueness under the narrower (strategy_id) key necessarily still satisfy it under the wider one, so the migration is safe on existing data with no preflight duplicate check needed (021's own preflight already established there were no duplicates to begin with). Confirmed no other code path assumes global strategy_id uniqueness (grepped every .table("strategy_deployments") call site; none queries or relies on at-most-one-row-per-strategy_id across all users). Extended tests/test_strategy_lifecycle_concurrency_postgres.py (the file 021's own regression tests live in) rather than duplicating its real-PostgreSQL harness: added test_044_rekeys_to_user_and_strategy_with_the_same_predicate (static check that 044 drops the old index and recreates it on (user_id, strategy_id) naming all nine live spellings), updated _ScratchWorld's hand-built index to the new composite shape (so the harness emulates what production actually carries post-044, not 021's superseded shape), and added two new real-Postgres tests: test_mkt04_a_second_subscriber_can_deploy_while_the_first_is_still_live (two DIFFERENT user_ids, same strategy_id, both live -- the actual bug, reproduced then fixed) and test_mkt04_the_same_user_still_cannot_double_deploy_the_same_strategy (negative control: the SAME user is still refused a second live deployment of the same strategy, proving 021's original protection survives the re-key). Full marketplace_pipeline / work01_command_durability / validation_sweep regression (421 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.

title: The market-data quality validator's default thresholds reject almost all real-shaped market data
evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named, and traced its real blast radius: OutlierDetector._z_score_filter/_iqr_filter (reached by default -- ValidationConfig.outlier_method defaults to Z_SCORE) computed their test against the RAW price/volume LEVEL of the whole window, then rejected the ENTIRE window on a single violation. market_data_contract.quality_report, strategy_operations, strategy_service and training_worker all REUSE this exact validator per their own docstrings -- this is not dead code, it sits on real production paths. Confirmed empirically (not just by reading): a realistic trending-price + log-normal-volume series (900 bars, the platform's typical window size) was rejected by the pre-fix z-score-on-levels check on every one of several random seeds tried, while the existing test suite's own 'clean, accepted' fixture (tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py's _pool()) is explicitly documented as a bounded SINE WAVE rather than anything resembling real market data, specifically to dodge this exact bug -- independent confirmation the defect is real and already known-about well enough to be worked around rather than fixed. Root cause: price and volume levels are both non-stationary (price trends/drifts, volume is approximately log-normal) by construction, so a z-score/IQR test against a non-stationary series' own mean/quantiles measures 'how far this point is from a mean the trend/burst itself moved', unrelated to whether any individual bar is actually anomalous. FIX: switched both _z_score_filter and _iqr_filter to bar-to-bar LOG-RETURNS (log(x_t/x_(t-1))) for close AND volume -- the standard transform that makes a trending/multiplicative series approximately stationary, which these tests require to mean anything. Percent-change returns were tried first and empirically still left volume's heavy right tail (ordinary volume bursts are large MULTIPLICATIVE swings) fat enough to trip the z-score on realistic data (2 violations in 30 seeds); log-returns resolved it completely (0/30). Also raised z_score_threshold 3.0->5.0 and iqr_multiplier 1.5->3.0 (both env-overridable via MARKET_DATA_Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD / MARKET_DATA_IQR_MULTIPLIER): rejecting a whole window on ANY single point beyond a per-comparison threshold has a false-positive rate that RISES WITH WINDOW SIZE regardless of what it's computed over -- for a 900-bar window, a per-point threshold calibrated for a single comparison (3 sigma / 1.5xIQR) is tripped by chance alone far more often than not; this is a general multiple-comparisons argument, not a dataset-specific calibration, and both new values were empirically verified (across 25-30 independent random seeds per method) to clear realistic trending+bursty-volume windows while STILL catching a genuine single-bar 50x price spike. Investigated the third remediation item ('make the gap threshold interval-aware') and found it already true of the current code, just not of what the ledger note assumed: GapHandler.handle's actual gap DETECTION already derives its threshold from the timeframe (`expected_diff = timedelta(minutes=_timeframe_to_minutes(timeframe)); gaps = time_diffs > expected_diff * 1.5`) -- the `max_gap_minutes` PARAMETER the caller passes in (ValidationConfig.max_gap_minutes, fixed at 5.0) is dead code, immediately overwritten by the measured gap value before it is ever read. Not a gap in this codebase's current behaviour, just an unused/confusingly-named parameter; left as-is since removing a dead parameter is outside this finding's scope and touches a shared signature. New tests/test_data02_outlier_detection_on_returns_not_levels.py (39 tests): 25 independent random seeds of realistic trending-price + bursty-volume data accepted (previously rejected); a genuine single-bar 50x spike still rejected; the existing sine-wave clean/spike fixtures still behave exactly as before (both directions, independently re-verified here); the same two properties for the non-default IQR method. Full regression: new suite + tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py + tests/test_market_data_contract.py + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (542 tests) clean except pre-existing, unrelated EmptyCategoryError collection errors (confirmed pre-existing/unrelated repeatedly this session) and the 2 pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
remaining_action: The two threshold VALUES (z_score_threshold=5.0, iqr_multiplier=3.0) are principled, empirically-verified-against-synthetic-data defaults, not a fit against this platform's own real historical return distributions -- this sandbox has no such data. The original audit's own remediation note separated 'validate on returns/log-returns' (done, this session) from 'widen or recalibrate thresholds against real historical distributions' (NOT done -- needs a session with access to real market data to fine-tune beyond the general multiple-comparisons correction applied here). Both new constants are env-overridable so this can happen without a code change.

title: Walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters, and several of its reported figures are hardcoded placeholders
evidence: Confirmed by reading run_walk_forward_analysis: self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history) was called ONCE before the loop and the resulting fixed parameter set was evaluated on every window's train AND test period -- a fixed strategy re-run on rolling windows, not walk-forward analysis. Investigating this surfaced a more fundamental, previously untracked defect (filed and fixed separately as BT-02, commit 29e319d): BacktestRuntime.run_backtest never used start_date/end_date to select data at all, so every window's backtest ran on byte-identical 'most recent bars' regardless of its own dates, which would have made even a correct per-window fit numerically meaningless. Fixed run_walk_forward_analysis (depends on BT-02) by adding _optimize_on_window: a copy of the caller's config with parameters[start_date/end_date] overridden to the window's own train period, dispatched through the same search method (_grid_search/_random_search/_bayesian_optimization/_genetic_algorithm) the caller chose, with the window's own trials kept OUT of self._optimization_history so one window cannot leak into another's fit or into the whole-period benchmark (the OPT-03-shaped cross-contamination, reintroduced inside one engine instance if not guarded against). Also fixed the three hardcoded report figures the finding names: _run_buy_hold_benchmark (was the literal total_return_pct=50.0/sharpe_ratio=1.0/max_drawdown=20.0 for every call) now fetches the strategy's own symbol/timeframe over the same window via BT-02's since_ms/until_ms and computes all three from the closes actually fetched, reporting computed=False/None rather than a fabricated number when the fetch fails; _calculate_beta (was the literal 1.0) now computes cov(strategy_returns, benchmark_returns)/var(benchmark_returns) from both backtests' own return series, returning None rather than 0.0/1.0 when there are too few paired observations or the benchmark has zero variance; complexity score (was the literal 0.8) now scales with the strategy's own tunable-parameter count (1.0 at zero parameters, 0.0 at a documented 10-parameter cap), matching the 'higher is better' convention every other component of the weighted score already uses. New tests/test_opt02_walk_forward_fits_per_window_and_report_figures_are_real.py (10 tests) against a deterministic, parameter- and window-dependent fake backtest_runtime: different windows provably choose different winning parameters (not merely 'ran without crashing'); the fitted parameters carry unchanged from train to test; two windows' calls carry two different date ranges (the BT-02 dependency, checked directly); buy & hold computes a real return/Sharpe/drawdown from a controlled price series and reports not-computed on empty data; beta computes exactly (2.0 for a strategy whose returns are exactly 2x the benchmark's) and is None on zero variance or too few observations; alpha/beta are both None together when the benchmark could not be measured; complexity varies from 1.0 to 0.0 with parameter count. One real bug the test suite itself caught before commit: the first _calculate_beta draft mixed np.cov's sample covariance (ddof=1) with np.var's population variance (ddof=0), scaling every beta by N/(N-1) for no reason -- caught because the exactly-2.0 test came back 2.4, fixed by aligning both to ddof=1. Full regression: test_save_performs_no_backtest.py + test_opt01_optimize_config_field_name.py + test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py + test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py + test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (100 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated import-pin failure confirmed via git-stash comparison to predate this change entirely); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
remaining_action: None identified at the code level for the two defects this finding names. The fix credits two commits: 29e319d (BT-02, the data-range prerequisite) and be82e3d (this finding's own per-window fitting and report-figure fixes). The validation_method field on OptimizationConfig (TIME_SERIES_CV/BLOCKED_CV/ROLLING_VALIDATION/WALK_FORWARD) is still read only for a log line in run_walk_forward_analysis and does not select a different windowing or fitting strategy -- that is a separate, smaller gap this pass did not scope in, since the finding's own title and remaining_action named only the per-window fitting and the hardcoded figures.

title: Optimization engine is a process-wide singleton that leaks one tenant's best parameters into another tenant's walk-forward/sensitivity results
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/backend/optimization_engine.py::get_optimization_engine and backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::get_backtest_runtime: both are plain module-level singletons (global _x; if _x is None: _x = X(); return _x). Grepped every call site in the repo (exactly two): backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py's POST /strategies/{id}/optimize and backend_app/routers/strategies.py's POST /walk-forward both called them directly, so every tenant's call shared the SAME OptimizationEngine instance and therefore the SAME _optimization_history list -- every one of run_walk_forward_analysis/run_sensitivity_analysis/run_monte_carlo_simulation/run_benchmark_comparison reads its 'best parameters' back via self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history), so a tenant whose call overlapped or ran back-to-back with another tenant's in the same process could have had that tenant's optimization results folded into their own. The shared backtest_runtime singleton compounded it: constructed once with the class defaults ($10,000 capital, 0.1% fees, 0.05% slippage), so both endpoints' submitted capital/fee/slippage/risk fields were accepted and then silently ignored -- confirmed this is the EXACT SAME bug class backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_backtest_runtime_for's own docstring already names and fixes for the plain (non-optimization) backtest endpoint (that fix's own comment explicitly calls out get_backtest_runtime() by name as the thing it is NOT calling, for this exact reason) -- the optimize/walk-forward endpoints had simply not received the same fix. Fixed both call sites the same way: new backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_optimization_engine_for(body) constructs a fresh OptimizationEngine() and a fresh BacktestRuntime(...) (from the request's own initial_capital/commission/slippage/risk_per_trade/max_drawdown/daily_loss_limit fields) per request; backend_app/routers/strategies.py's /walk-forward closure does the equivalent inline, reusing the values already read into its OptimizationConfig (so no duplicate payload.get() calls). get_optimization_engine()/get_backtest_runtime() themselves are UNCHANGED -- kept, not deleted, since tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's Requirement-22.1 tripwire still needs to patch get_backtest_runtime by name in both router modules to prove a strategy SAVE never starts a backtest. Removed a redundant local re-import of OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime inside /walk-forward's closure that would otherwise have shadowed the module-level names and silently defeated test patching at the new injection points. New tests/test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py (6 tests, direct construction, no mocking -- mirrors tests/test_task_6_1_backtest_execute.py's existing proof pattern for the sibling bug): two calls return two different engine instances with independent _optimization_history (the concrete cross-tenant leak, reproduced then shown closed); the runtime carries the SUBMITTED capital/fee/slippage/risk values, not the class defaults; two different configurations produce two differently-configured runtimes; the engine returned is wired to THIS call's own runtime; the singleton accessors themselves are unchanged and still work (negative control). title: Marketplace browse builds a PostgREST filter from raw user input
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/library.py::browse_library: the `q` search parameter was interpolated raw into a PostgREST or() filter string -- query.or_(f"name.ilike.%{q}%,description.ilike.%{q}%") -- and PostgREST's filter mini-language treats `,`, `.`, `(`, `)` as syntax, so a search term containing any of them could close the current clause and open a new one against an unrelated column. Separately, the handler fetched ALL matching rows via query.execute() and sliced [offset:offset+limit] in Python, so every browse request transferred the entire matching catalogue regardless of page size. Fixed both. (1) Extracted _postgrest_quoted_ilike_pattern(term): wraps the term in double quotes (PostgREST's own escaping rule), backslash-escaping \ and " themselves FIRST -- in that order, deliberately, since escaping quotes before doubling backslashes would let a trailing backslash absorb its own escaping backslash and leave the closing quote unescaped. (2) Switched to count="exact" on .select() plus .range(offset, offset+limit-1) on the query, pushing LIMIT/OFFSET and the total-match count to PostgREST instead of this process. Extended two existing fake-Supabase test doubles (tests/test_marketplace_pipeline.py::FakeTable, tests/test_library_detail_projection_regression.py::_Query/_Resp) with .range()/count="exact" support, since neither had it before this fix and both are exercised by this same handler's existing regression suite. New tests/test_api08_browse_search_term_is_escaped.py (9 tests): the pure escaping function round-trips a plain term, each of the four reserved characters, a term attempting to break out via literal double quotes, and a trailing-backslash ordering-sensitivity case (verified against an independently-written unescaper, not just 'whatever the function produces'); an end-to-end request with reserved characters in q no longer errors; pagination through the real route returns the requested page and an accurate total count sourced from PostgREST, not len() over everything. tests/test_marketplace_pipeline.py, test_library_detail_projection_regression.py, test_listing_projection.py and 3 other library/marketplace test files (633 tests total) still pass -- test_listing_projection.py's own static sweep for unprojected Listing-row leaks required restating the total-count computation as max(page_result.count or 0, len(paginated)) rather than a ternary, since its row-content taint tracker only exempts a handful of row-REDUCING call names (len, sum, min, max, ...) when they are the ENTIRE assigned expression, not a ternary branch.

title: Notifications are kept in an unbounded per-process dict with an O(n) idempotency scan
evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named: backend_app/routers/notifications.py's _in_memory_notifications was a plain, unbounded module-level dict -- one entry retained forever for every notification ever created in this process's lifetime, across every tenant, whether or not it was ALSO durably persisted to Supabase (list_notifications always tries Supabase first and only falls back to this dict when Supabase has nothing, confirmed by reading it -- so a persisted entry's in-memory copy was pure, unbounded-growth dead weight). The idempotency check also did a full scan (`for existing_id, existing_data in _in_memory_notifications.items(): ...`) on every single create, so it got slower, not just memory-hungrier, as the dict grew. Fixed with (1) _MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS (env-overridable via MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS, default 5000) -- once exceeded, the OLDEST entries are evicted (plain dicts preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+, and no code here ever re-inserts an existing key, so the first key is reliably the oldest); (2) an O(1) idempotency index (_idempotency_index, keyed by (user_id, idempotency_key)) replacing the full-dict scan, kept in sync on insert, eviction, AND delete (both delete_notification and delete_all_notifications now route through a shared _forget_notification_locked helper instead of a bare `del`, so a deleted or evicted notification's idempotency key is freed for reuse rather than left dangling). New tests/test_hy04_notifications_memory_bounded.py (6 tests, using a shrunk cap via monkeypatch rather than actually inserting 5000+ rows) proves: exceeding the cap evicts the oldest entries first; a duplicate idempotency key for the SAME user returns the existing id without growing the store; the SAME key for DIFFERENT users does not collide; delete_notification and delete_all_notifications both clean the idempotency index, not just the dict; an evicted entry's idempotency key is freed for reuse. Updated tests/test_notifications_feature_e2e.py's state-cleanup fixture to also clear the new _idempotency_index between tests (it only cleared _in_memory_notifications before, which would have let the new index leak across runs in that file's own autouse fixture -- a miniature version of the exact unbounded-growth problem this finding is about). Full regression (new HY-04 suite + existing notifications e2e suite, 1 file/23+ tests + tests/test_validation_sweep.py, 388+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session (missing real Supabase service credentials in this sandbox).
remaining_action: The finding's remediation note offered TWO options joined by 'and/or': cap the in-memory structure, OR make Supabase the source of truth with a visible degraded-mode indicator. This fix takes the first option in full (bounded growth, O(1) idempotency) -- the second option's 'visible degraded-mode indicator' (e.g. surfacing to the user or to ops when notifications are running on the in-memory fallback rather than Supabase) was NOT attempted; Supabase was already and remains the primary store attempted first on every write and read, so this is an observability nice-to-have on top of an already-correct fallback, not a remaining correctness gap.

title: Referral payout debit and payout insert are two non-transactional writes with best-effort compensation; payout completion is unimplemented
evidence: This finding has three asks; two are fixed this session, the hardest (full transactionality) is deliberately deferred. (1) 'fail closed on lock-acquisition error': confirmed backend_app/routers/referral.py::create_payout_request's lock-acquire except clause did `lock_acquired = True` on any exception -- fail OPEN. Traced through core/cache/redis_manager.py::SharedRedisManager.set(), which is itself deliberately fail-soft (swallows every exception and returns False, never raises), confirming this except clause is currently DEAD CODE -- but a landmine: RED-01's own remaining_action (still OPEN) proposes making redis_manager raise for exactly this class of safety-gate caller, and if that lands, this dead branch would silently come alive and reintroduce the double-spend race it exists to prevent. Changed to `lock_acquired = False` -- fail closed under either implementation. The wallet's own atomic conditional UPDATE (.gte('approved_balance_usd', ...)) remains the real correctness backstop regardless of this lock, confirmed by reading it: two concurrent requests race on the SAME conditional UPDATE, and Postgres serializes it row-wise, so only one can ever match: failing closed here only costs a confusing-but-safe 'please wait' on a genuine Redis outage, never a double-spend. (2) 'implement the pending->completed settlement step': grepped the whole file for the word 'completed' before this fix and found zero writes of it anywhere -- a payout request could be created and then sit in 'pending' forever with no code path to mark it done or refused. New PUT /api/referral/payouts/{id}/settle, admin-gated (get_admin_user) and running under the service-role client (get_service_supabase, via Depends -- confirmed referral_payouts and referral_wallets both carry an owner-only RLS policy, user_id = auth.uid(), so an admin's own JWT cannot read or write a payout or wallet belonging to the user being settled; this is the SEC-08 pattern this codebase already uses for platform actions on another tenant's rows). 'completed' requires an external reference (the operator attests they performed the transfer manually -- there is no outbound payment-rail integration anywhere in this codebase for referral payouts, only inbound Stripe/Razorpay webhooks, so this correctly does not claim to move money itself) and records processed_at. 'rejected' re-credits the wallet balance create_payout_request's own debit had already taken out, reading the CURRENT balance and adding back the payout amount (not blindly restoring a stale snapshot) -- without this, a rejected payout would leave the money permanently unaccounted for. An already-terminal payout (completed/rejected) cannot be settled again (409, via an optimistic .eq('status', <expected>) guard on the update, the same CAS style the debit itself already uses). New tests/test_ref01_payout_lock_fails_closed.py (2 tests): a lock-acquisition error refuses the payout (409) and -- the actual correctness property -- NEVER reaches the debit step at all. New tests/test_ref01_payout_settlement.py (6 tests): a non-admin is refused before touching the database; completing records the reference and does NOT touch the wallet; completing with no reference is refused (400) and does not mutate the payout; rejecting re-credits the wallet by exactly the payout amount; an already-settled payout cannot be settled again for either terminal status. Updated tests/test_validation_sweep.py with a MutatingRoute entry for the new endpoint (the sweep's own completeness check caught the omission) and fixed a now-stale comment in tests/test_referral_payout_debit_is_compensated_on_insert_failure.py's harness fixture that described the pre-fix fail-open behaviour. title: The API client overwrites caller-supplied Idempotency-Key headers with its own weak hash
evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/src/apiClient.js's request interceptor: it called generateIdempotencyKey(config.url, data), which hashed sessionId_url_payloadStr with a weak 32-bit simpleHash into the Idempotency-Key header UNCONDITIONALLY -- even when the caller (api/modules/strategies.js::deploy's options.idempotencyKey, a prepared but not-yet-wired-to-any-UI call site) had already set its own Idempotency-Key header, it was overwritten. The deeper bug: the hash was deterministic over (session, url, payload), so two SEPARATE, deliberately-identical submissions (placing the same order twice in a row on purpose) collided onto the identical key, and the backend's own idempotency check would then treat the second legitimate order as a duplicate retry of the first. Fixed: the interceptor now checks config.headers['Idempotency-Key'] for an existing value first and only falls back to its own generator when the caller supplied none; the fallback itself (generateIdempotencyKey) no longer takes url/data at all -- it is now idemp_${crypto.randomUUID()}, content-independent, so two identical submissions never collide. Removed simpleHash (now unused) and getSessionId (now unused -- confirmed no other call site anywhere in algo22-terminal/src or tests references either name). New algo22-terminal/tests/unit/apiClientIdempotencyFe05.test.js (4 tests, same axios-mock convention as the existing ATTACK 3 idempotency test it extends): a caller-supplied key is honoured verbatim, not overwritten; a request with no caller key still gets a defined idemp_-prefixed key; two identical submissions with no caller key get DIFFERENT keys (the collision bug, proven fixed); a GET request still never receives the header. The pre-existing tests/unit/attack_frontend_full.test.js (8 tests, whose ATTACK 3 only asserted the idemp_ prefix and definedness, not hash-determinism) still passes.
remaining_action: No current UI call site actually passes options.idempotencyKey to strategies.deploy (or any other caller-supplied-key path) yet -- this fix makes the mechanism correct for when one is wired up, consistent with how this session treated other prepared-but-unused mechanisms (e.g. SEC-11). A future session adding a 'Deploy' button's retry/resubmit handling should generate one UUID per click and pass it through, rather than relying on this interceptor's own per-request fallback, if intentional retry-coalescing is wanted.

title: The secret-redacting log filter is installed on only 13 marketplace/paper logger names; billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers are unfiltered
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/observability.py: RedactingLogFilter was attached only to the 13 logger names in GUARDED_LOGGER_NAMES (task 33.4's own scope: marketplace and paper) -- billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers carried no secret redaction at all. A Logger's own filters apply only to records it originates (Logger.handle checks self.filters, never an ancestor's), which is why attaching to 13 named loggers protected only those 13 and nothing else, however many other loggers exist in the codebase. Added install_root_log_redaction(), which attaches RedactingLogFilter to every HANDLER on the root logger instead -- a Handler's filters run for every record that propagates to it, whatever logger originated it, which is the mechanism the remediation note ("Install RedactingLogFilter at the root logging handler") names precisely. main.py calls it immediately after its own logging.basicConfig(...), which is what gives the root logger a handler to attach to. The original module's own docstring explains WHY root-handler attachment was avoided for task 33.4 ("redact the whole process's output, which the task forbids") -- that was a deliberate narrow scope for that task, not a permanent prohibition, and LOG-01 is exactly the later finding asking for the wider behavior that task declined. New tests/test_log01_root_redaction_covers_every_logger.py (4 tests, using a standalone logger/handler pair, never the real process root): an arbitrary, never-individually-guarded logger name is redacted once the handler it propagates to carries the filter; a record from an ALREADY-guarded logger (PaperRepository) is proven not to be double-mangled by passing through both its own logger filter and the root handler filter (the second pass on already-redacted text is a no-op); the installer is idempotent; a handler-less logger (the real root before basicConfig runs) returns 0 rather than raising. tests/test_log_redaction.py (362 tests, pre-existing) still passes; confirmed main.py still imports and boots with the root handler now carrying the filter.
remaining_action: Covers the single root handler logging.basicConfig installs, the dominant real log path for this process (every logger with propagate=True, the default, eventually reaches it). Does not retroactively cover a handler some other module attaches directly to a non-root logger and removes from the propagation chain (propagate=False), nor a handler uvicorn or another framework might attach to the root AFTER main.py's own install_root_log_redaction() call runs -- neither case was found by reading main.py, but a dedicated audit of every logging.basicConfig/addHandler call site was not performed. Two pre-existing, unrelated test failures (test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py's EXCH-01 sandbox-refusal mismatch, test_task_33_2_rate_limit_keys.py's rate-limit-count test) were confirmed to reproduce identically on the unmodified baseline via git stash -- not caused by this fix, not fixed by it either.

title: The distributed rate limiter fails open on any Redis error
evidence: Confirmed the fail-open pattern in two layers: backend_app/core/distributed_rate_limiter.py::DistributedRateLimiter.check_rate_limit ("Fail-safe: allow request on error" -> allowed=True unconditionally on ANY exception, including a Redis outage) and backend_app/core/exchange_rate_limiter.py::DistributedRateLimiterIntegration.check_user_rate_limit (same pattern, one layer up, catching failures above check_rate_limit itself). IMPORTANT REACHABILITY FINDING: traced every caller and confirmed NEITHER layer is reached by any live request today. DistributedRateLimiterIntegration is called only by its own sibling method (acquire_user_quota) in the same class, never from outside exchange_rate_limiter.py; exchange_rate_limiter.py's own exchange_limiter singleton/exchange_limited decorator/ExchangeRateLimiter class are never imported anywhere else either. The actual live protection against an exchange ban is ccxt's own built-in enableRateLimit: True, set directly in both exchange_executor.py and connection_engine.py -- purely in-process, no Redis dependency, no fail-open-on-external-failure risk at all. Fixed anyway, same reasoning as SEC-11 (a fail-open landmine in an unreached module becomes a live bug the moment something is wired up to call it): both except blocks now fail CLOSED specifically for the one rate-limit type/operation this module's own vocabulary ties to venue-ban risk (RateLimitType.ORDERS_PER_MINUTE / operation="orders"), matching the remediation note's own distinction, and fail open for the cosmetic/UI-facing types (signals, API calls, WebSocket connections) as the note explicitly says may remain acceptable. get_status() (read-only, "without consuming quota" per its own docstring, not an enforcement gate) and reset() (operator action) were left untouched -- neither is a decision point this finding is about. New tests/test_rl01_rate_limiter_fails_closed_for_orders.py (7 tests): ORDERS_PER_MINUTE denies on a simulated Redis outage; the three cosmetic types still fail open on the same outage (negative control); a healthy Redis still allows an under-limit order (negative control, not a blanket deny); the exchange_rate_limiter.py layer denies "orders" and still allows "signals" on an equivalent failure one level up. tests/test_exchange_rate_limiter.py (9 tests, pre-existing -- covers the actually-live TokenBucket/ExchangeRateLimiter classes, untouched by this fix) still passes.
remaining_action: The module this finding targets is currently dead code in the live order-placement path (see evidence) -- this fix closes the landmine without changing any current production behavior. A future session should decide whether to delete backend_app/core/distributed_rate_limiter.py and the unused parts of exchange_rate_limiter.py entirely (ccxt's enableRateLimit already covers the real need with no distributed-coordination gap, since each pod throttles its own calls to the SAME per-pod ccxt client instance per exchange connection -- whether that is sufficient across multiple pods sharing one exchange account's global limit was not investigated here and is a separate, not-yet-tracked question), or wire DistributedRateLimiterIntegration into a real call site if genuine cross-pod coordination of exchange-venue calls is still wanted.

title: Checkout currency/country detection trusts client-controllable headers, but the actual pricing impact is narrow
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/country_detection.py: extract_client_ip unconditionally trusted CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For, and detect_country_from_headers unconditionally trusted CloudFront-Viewer-Country and CF-IPCountry -- a caller that reaches this process directly, bypassing whichever CDN is supposed to set these (this deployment's own terraform does not describe a CloudFront/ALB topology at all -- INF-02), could set any of them to anything and get a different region's price list via pricing_service.py::determine_pricing_context's IP-detection tier. Traced the actual commercial impact and confirmed the finding's own 'narrow' framing: determine_pricing_context's step 3 (an explicit currency_override query param) already takes highest precedence over IP/header detection, so a user can already pick any supported currency outright -- spoofing the geo header is a stealthier route to a capability that already exists overtly, not a new one. Fixed the header-trust half anyway, reusing the house pattern SEC-10 already built for this exact question ('is there a real proxy chain in front of this process') rather than inventing a second one: added client_address.trusted_edge_is_configured() (True only when TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is a valid >=1 integer, the same fail-safe-by-default check trusted_client_address's own hop count already uses for rate-limit keys) and gated every one of the six headers above on it in country_detection.py. Unconfigured (this sandbox's default, and the fail-safe default for any deployment that has not explicitly confirmed its proxy topology), none of the six headers can change the detected IP or country any more -- detection falls through to the direct socket peer and the deterministic US/USD fallback. New tests/test_geo01_edge_headers_require_trusted_proxy.py (16 tests): trusted_edge_is_configured tracks TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS exactly as trusted_client_address's internal hop count does; each of the six headers is proven ignored with TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS unset, including the one case that actually matters commercially (a spoofed CloudFront-Viewer-Country against an unconfigured deployment resolves to US/USD, not the attacker-chosen country); a negative control proves every header still works once TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is set, so this is a default, not a removal. Updated tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py's five existing header-trust tests to set TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS (the deployment-has-confirmed-its-topology case they were already written to exercise) and added a new TestEdgeHeadersUntrustedByDefault class (6 tests) proving the previously-undefended default. Full tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py + test_production_payment_e2e_acceptance.py + SEC-10/REF-02/SEC-12/validation_sweep/route_contract regression (399 passed) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
remaining_action: The header-trust root cause is closed for every deployment that has not explicitly confirmed TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS -- which, per INF-02, describes this platform's actual production deployment today (no terraform describes its real topology, so there is nothing here to tell this code whether a CDN really fronts it). Once an operator sets TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS for the real topology, trust resumes exactly as before this fix -- a CloudFront origin-request policy that strips or validates these headers at the edge (this finding's own remediation note) is still the stronger, infrastructure-level fix and was not attempted: this session has no AWS credentials to configure CloudFront, and INF-02 already records that the repo's terraform does not describe the live distribution to configure a policy against. The remediation note's other half (keep FX rates fresher than the hardcoded baseline fallback) is a separate concern already owned by fx_service.py's own live-rate/cache/stale-grace/baseline tiers, unchanged here, and not re-verified in this pass.

title: The admin-only portfolio-management API is largely non-functional (unawaited coroutines, nested-lock deadlock risk)
evidence: The three asks in the original remaining_action (add missing awaits; fix the non-reentrant lock being re-entered; fix forced_reduction's close percentage) were the tip of a much deeper problem: this module (admin-only, mounted at /api/internal/portfolio-mgmt behind get_admin_user, confirmed separate from the real live-trading routers/portfolio.py) had ZERO prior behavioral test coverage anywhere in the repo, and crashed or hung at nearly every call site once actually exercised. Found and fixed, layer by layer, by actually calling the code rather than reading it: (1) validate_consistency() was called from both open_position and close_position but was never defined ANYWHERE on PortfolioManager -- AttributeError on every single open or close, before any other bug was even reached. Implemented it for real: checks each strategy's used_capital+available_capital==allocated_capital invariant and that open_positions/strategy_positions only reference live, correctly-filed positions. (2) Missing awaits on get_margin_metrics/_check_exposure_limits/register_strategy and several GET endpoints (exposure/margin/margin/health/margin/status/pnl/detailed-summary/prices/update) -- all returned unexecuted coroutine objects instead of data. (3) asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: get_portfolio_summary held its own lock and then called three other lock-acquiring methods; open_position's conflict-cancellation step called the lock-acquiring close_position while already holding that lock; update_prices did the same into margin_monitor.check_margin_health -> _forced_position_reduction -> close_position. All three are guaranteed deadlocks the moment missing-await bug #2 is fixed first (which is presumably why nobody had hit this in whatever manual testing existed). Fixed by splitting get_margin_metrics/get_exposure_metrics/get_pnl_summary/_check_exposure_limits/close_position into `_locked` bodies the caller can invoke directly while already holding the lock, with public async wrappers that acquire it fresh; narrowed update_prices' own lock scope so the margin check and any resulting forced liquidation run after the price-update lock is released. (4) get_exposure_metrics built an ExposureMetrics() instance and then read/wrote MarginMetrics-shaped fields on it (margin_used, margin_level, margin_call_threshold...) that ExposureMetrics does not declare as fields at all -- AttributeError on every call where margin_used<=0, i.e. an EMPTY portfolio, the ordinary starting state. This was a copy-paste of the margin calculation onto the wrong dataclass; rewrote it to populate ExposureMetrics' own real fields (symbol/strategy exposure breakdown, gross/net/long/short exposure, leverage, concentration), which is also the shape every caller (get_portfolio_summary, create_snapshot) already assumed when reading .symbol_exposure/.gross_exposure off the result. (5) create_snapshot (called from inside open_position/close_position, i.e. on every trade) read self.pm.available_capital/self.pm.used_capital, neither of which exists on PortfolioManager at all (only per-strategy StrategyAllocation.available_capital/used_capital do) -- AttributeError on every single snapshot. Fixed to sum across self.pm.allocations.values(). Also fixed create_snapshot's exposure_metrics.total_exposure read (ExposureMetrics has no such field either) to use the real gross_exposure field. (6) MarginMonitor's forced-liquidation path called self.pm.close_position(position_id=..., close_price=..., reason=...) -- but close_position's parameter is named exit_price, not close_price -- TypeError on every forced liquidation. Fixed, and made check_margin_health/_forced_position_reduction/get_margin_status async so they can properly await the manager calls they depend on (they were plain sync methods calling async methods, which can never actually run the async body). (7) the liquidation log said 'reducing by 25%' while the code's own comment admits there is no partial-close method and it always closes the entire position -- an operator reading logs during a real margin event would see a false 'only trimmed 25%' when 100% was actually liquidated. The log and the result's 'action' field now both say 'full_close', matching what actually happens. New tests/test_pm01_portfolio_manager_is_functional.py (8 tests, every call that used to deadlock wrapped in asyncio.wait_for with a 5s timeout so a regression times out loudly instead of hanging the whole suite) exercises register_strategy, open_position (including the real conflict-cancellation path with two opposing positions), close_position, update_prices, a real forced-liquidation scenario (drives an actual margin_level under the 110% threshold and asserts the position is actually closed, not just logged about), and get_portfolio_summary/get_margin_status end to end. Full regression (new suite + every other portfolio-management test in the repo + validation_sweep, 450+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
remaining_action: True partial position reduction (closing e.g. 25% of a position's size rather than always closing 100%) is NOT implemented -- PortfolioManager has no partial-close primitive (resizing a Position's quantity while keeping it open and correctly re-deriving its realized/unrealized PnL split) and adding one is a real feature, not a bug fix, with its own design and test surface. This pass fixed the DISHONESTY (claiming 25% while doing 100%) and the crashes/deadlocks around it, not the missing feature -- always closing fully on a liquidation-risk margin event is a conservative, safe behavior, not an unsafe one, so this is a legitimate deferral rather than a masked defect.

title: Alembic's baseline migration DROPs core trading tables; running it against an existing, unstamped production database would destroy data
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/alembic/versions/4ef23035a692_baseline.py: it has no down_revision -- the first thing alembic upgrade head runs against an unstamped database -- and its upgrade() unconditionally DROP TABLE ... CASCADEs orders, positions, fills, transaction_records, transaction_checkpoints, transaction_rollbacks and idempotency_keys. On a fresh database this is a no-op; against an EXISTING, unstamped production database (this platform's own parallel raw-SQL migration system, backend_app/migrations/*.sql, already creates orders/positions/fills independently of Alembic, with real rows), running it would silently destroy every one of them. Added _refuse_if_any_target_table_has_rows(bind), called as the FIRST statement in upgrade() before any DROP: checks all seven target tables for even one row (EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM ... LIMIT 1), not a full COUNT) and raises, having altered nothing, naming every populated table and pointing the operator at alembic stamp 4ef23035a692 as the actual next step, per the remediation note. A table that does not exist yet (the fresh-database case this revision was written for) is skipped, not flagged. New tests/test_db_alm01_baseline_refuses_on_populated_tables.py (5 tests, real SQLite engine, loaded by path same as scripts/-style files): a populated table trips the guard and leaves its row in place; an EMPTY existing table does not (negative control -- not "refuse if the table exists"); a nonexistent table does not (negative control -- the fresh-database case); multiple populated tables are all named, not just the first; and a source-inspection check proves the guard call is literally the first statement in upgrade(), ahead of every op.execute DROP -- not merely defined and never called. tests/test_bug049_sql_and_alembic_agree.py (15 tests, pre-existing, also inspects this versions/ directory) still passes.

title: Two independent sequence allocators for paper session events can collide and drop a bar on feed disconnect
evidence: Confirmed the collision mechanism exactly as named: paper_market_feed.FeedHandle._emit_feed_disconnected allocated its sequence from paper_repository.next_session_event_sequence (max(paper_events.sequence) + 1, read off the LOG), while every other Paper_Channel event (paper_events.record_event -> next_sequence -> paper_repository.allocate_session_event_sequence) allocates from an atomic compare-and-swap on the paper_sessions.event_sequence COUNTER. Traced the actual failure mode: the feed writer's INSERT (via insert_session_event) advances the LOG but never touches the COUNTER, so a subsequent ordinary event's counter-based allocation can read a stale, lower number and collide with the sequence the feed writer already used; uq_paper_event_seq then refuses that ordinary event's INSERT with PaperDuplicateSessionEvent, and neither paper_session_service._emit nor the bar-stepping loop that calls it catches or retries that exception -- so the bar is dropped, not merely delayed. Fixed by routing _emit_feed_disconnected through allocate_session_event_sequence instead, so there is only one source of truth for the next sequence number and the race cannot happen at all. next_session_event_sequence itself is kept (it has its own direct test coverage and tests/property/test_paper_channel_sequence.py reuses it as a synthetic log-based second writer to stress-test the counter allocator's retry logic in general) -- only its one production caller moved. Along the way, fixed a stale property test harness bug this change exposed: tests/test_paper_market_feed_selection.py's shared _session_row() fixture never carried an event_sequence key at all, and the fake client's eq-filter compares str(row.get(col)) against the literal given -- an ABSENT key reads back as 'None', which never equals '0', so allocate_session_event_sequence's own compare-and-swap would lose all three attempts against this fixture even though the real column defaults the row to exactly the value the swap expects. Seeded it at 0 (the column's real DEFAULT per migration 009), which is behaviourally transparent to every other reader (the allocator's own code already treats an absent/NULL value as 0) and only matters for this exact-string-equality fake match. Updated the two stale docstring claims in test_paper_channel_sequence.py that called next_session_event_sequence 'task 24.4's feed writer's allocator ... a real production path', which is no longer true after this fix. New tests/test_paper06_feed_disconnect_shares_the_allocator.py (3 tests): an AST check that the feed-disconnect writer's own source calls allocate_session_event_sequence and not next_session_event_sequence (catches a revert even without a live collision); a real disconnect advances the counter to exactly match the log's own highest sequence (they can no longer diverge); and the exact scenario this finding describes -- a disconnect immediately followed by an ordinary event -- allocates consecutive, non-colliding sequence numbers end to end, with both rows landing. Full regression: the new suite + every paper-trading test in the repo (tests/ -k paper, 1590 passed) + test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed), clean except 2 unrelated pre-existing EmptyCategoryError collection failures (confirmed pre-existing and unrelated earlier this session, e.g. test_dag_hash_sensitivity.py) and the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
